lede: A race timer finds that one of sixteen swim times was typed wrongly. The times themselves were never kept, only their mean and standard deviation. Nothing is lost: both rest on two totals, and a total can be edited where a mean cannot. Fix the totals, then recompute.
can: Tell a correction, a removal and an addition apart by what happens to the count
Edit $\sum x$ by the values and $\sum x^{2}$ by their squares
Recompute the mean and standard deviation, and check which way each should move

text: A change edits the totals, never the mean

md: A mean cannot be edited: it is a total already shared out. The total behind it can be rebuilt, $\sum x = n\bar{x}$, and edited. So when one value was wrong, leaves, or joins, change the totals and recompute. Name the change first: a correction keeps the count, a removal lowers it by one, and an addition raises it by one.

title: Why the count decides so much
md: The count is the divisor in both formulas, the mean and the standard deviation. Get it wrong once and every later line inherits it, however good the arithmetic.

stem: 16 swimmers' times had a mean of 41 seconds. One time was recorded as 36 seconds when it was really 44 seconds. Find the corrected mean.

steps.decision: Rebuild the total: the mean times the count.
The wrong time comes out and the right one goes in. Both move.
A correction keeps all 16 times, so divide by 16.

prompt: 25 values have $\sum x = 1250$. One value was recorded as 47 when it was really 62. What is the corrected $\sum x$?
explain: As in step 2 of See it, take the wrong value out and put the right one in: $1250 - 47 + 62 = 1265$. Adding 62 alone would count 26 values.

twin.prompt: 20 values have $\sum x = 840$. A value recorded as 75 should have been 57. What is the corrected $\sum x$?

md: The standard deviation needs $\sum x^{2}$, and a question gives only $n$, $\bar{x}$ and $\sigma$. Turn the sheet's formula round: the variance is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean, so the mean of the squares is $\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}$, and $n$ times that is the total.

title: Two lines before anything else
md: Every question in this topic starts the same way: $\sum x = n\bar{x}$ and $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$. Write both before you read what changed.

stem: Rearrange the sheet's formula for $\sum x^{2}$, then use it on the 16 swim times, whose standard deviation was 3 seconds.

steps.decision: Square both sides of the sheet's formula.
Add $\bar{x}^{2}$ to both sides, then multiply by $n$.
Both terms: without $\sigma^{2}$ the times would have no spread at all.

prompt: 20 values have a mean of 35 and a standard deviation of 4. What is $\sum x^{2}$?
explain: As in step 2 of See it, $\sum x^{2} = 20\left(4^{2} + 35^{2}\right) = 20 \times 1241 = 24820$. Without the $4^{2}$ it would be 24500, a set with no spread.

twin.prompt: 15 values have a mean of 22 and a standard deviation of 3. What is $\sum x^{2}$?

text: Why the squares move by squares

md: A sum of squares holds each value's own square. When a value changes from $a$ to $b$, its square $a^{2}$ leaves and $b^{2}$ arrives, so $\sum x^{2}$ moves by $b^{2} - a^{2}$. The Summer 2025 report saw sums of squares moved by the square of the difference, $(b - a)^{2}$, instead; the raw difference $b - a$ is no better.

stem: Three values, 2, 5 and 8, have the 5 corrected to 9. Find the new sum of squares two ways.

steps.decision: The sum of squares as recorded.
Worked out again from the corrected values.
The edit gives the same total: $5^{2}$ out, $9^{2}$ in. Adding 4, or $4^{2} = 16$, would not.

prompt: One value in a set is corrected from 7 to 12. By how much does $\sum x^{2}$ go up?
explain: As in step 3 of See it, the old square leaves and the new one arrives: $12^{2} - 7^{2} = 144 - 49 = 95$. Neither 5 nor $5^{2} = 25$ is the change.

md: With both totals edited, the sheet's formula runs again on the corrected totals, over the same count, with the corrected mean. The old mean belongs to the old data: using it measures the spread about the wrong centre. Keep the corrected mean unrounded when it is not exact.

stem: Find the corrected standard deviation of the 16 swim times.

steps.decision: Squares out, squares in.
Same count, corrected mean.
With the old mean, 41, it would be $\sqrt{1730 - 1681} = 7$: far too big.

prompt: After a correction, 10 values have $\sum x = 620$ and $\sum x^{2} = 38810$. What is the corrected standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
explain: As in steps 2 and 3 of See it: the corrected mean is $\dfrac{620}{10} = 62$, then $\dfrac{38810}{10} - 62^{2} = 3881 - 3844 = 37$, and $\sqrt{37} = 6.08$.

twin.prompt: After a correction, 12 values have $\sum x = 300$ and $\sum x^{2} = 7660$. What is the standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: The mean is 25, so $638.33 - 625 = 13.33$, and its root is 3.65.

text: A removal: the count comes down

md: When a value leaves, three things change: the count falls by one, $\sum x$ loses the value and $\sum x^{2}$ loses its square. Divide by the new count from then on: it is the number of values the question now describes.
Read the question's words for the kind of change. Disqualified, withdrawn or struck out means a removal; joined or added means an addition; recorded wrongly or should have been means a correction.

stem: 12 runners had a mean time of 50 minutes and a standard deviation of 6 minutes. The runner who took 61 minutes is removed. Find the mean and standard deviation of the other 11.

steps.decision: Rebuild both totals for all 12.
The value leaves the sum, its square leaves the sum of squares, and the count falls.
Divide by 11.
The new count and the new mean in the sheet's formula.

prompt: 15 values have a mean of 28. The value 42 is removed. What is the mean of the values left?
explain: As in steps 2 and 3 of See it: $\dfrac{15 \times 28 - 42}{14} = \dfrac{378}{14} = 27$. Dividing by 15 would forget that one value has gone.

text: An addition: the count goes up

md: An addition runs the other way: the count rises by one, $\sum x$ gains the new value and $\sum x^{2}$ gains its square. A value well away from the mean widens the spread; one close to it narrows it slightly.

stem: 8 seedlings had a mean height of 14 cm and a standard deviation of 2 cm. A ninth seedling, 23 cm tall, is added. Find the new mean and standard deviation.

steps.decision: Rebuild both totals for the 8.
The new value, its square, and one more in the count.
Divide by 9.
From 2 to 3.40: the new seedling sits 9 cm from the mean.

prompt: Nine values have $\sum x = 189$ and $\sum x^{2} = 4080$. A tenth value, 31, is added. What is the new standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
explain: As in steps 2 to 4 of See it: now $\sum x = 220$, $\sum x^{2} = 4080 + 961 = 5041$ and $n = 10$, so the mean is 22 and $\sqrt{504.1 - 484} = \sqrt{20.1} = 4.48$.

twin.prompt: Seven values have $\sum x = 91$ and $\sum x^{2} = 1267$. An eighth value, 13, is added. What is the new standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?

text: Exam twists: the count and the pair

md: **Rebuild with the right count.** Summer 2025 asked for the corrected mean of fifteen jumps, and some multiplied the mean by 14. A correction keeps every value, so the count is the number the question names.
**Use both values.** Many in the same year adjusted with only one of the two numbers. The wrong value comes out and the right one goes in: one without the other loses or doubles an item.
**Square the right thing.** The same report saw $\sum x$ squared where $\sum x^{2}$ was needed. $\left(\sum x\right)^{2}$ squares the total; $\sum x^{2}$ adds the squares, and it is far smaller.

stem: 24 readings had a mean of 18.5. One was recorded as 16 when it was 22. Start the corrected total.

steps.decision: All 24 readings are still there: multiply by 24, not 23.
Both values move, and the count stays at 24.

prompt: 15 throws had a mean of 46 m. One was recorded as 41 m when it was 53 m. Which line starts the corrected total correctly?
explain: As in step 1 of See it, all 15 throws are still in the set, so the total is the mean times 15. The 41 then comes out and the 53 goes in.

twin.prompt: 20 times had a mean of 11 s. One was recorded as 9 s when it was 14 s. Which corrected total is right?
twin.explain: All 20 times stay; the wrong time comes out and the right one goes in.

optionNotes.why: The 9 was never taken out, so one time is counted twice.
Nothing has left the set, so the total is rebuilt from all 20 times.
That rebuilds the total from 14 throws. A correction removes nothing, so all 15 are still counted.
The right throw has gone in but the wrong one is still there, so 16 throws are counted. Take 41 out too.

text: Exam twists: every value off together

md: **One mistake in every value.** A scale that reads 3 too high moves every value, and the mean, by 3. The gaps between the values do not move, so the standard deviation stays as it was. Summer 2024 saw the change added to, or taken from, the standard deviation as well.

caption: Every value moves 3, so the mean moves 3; the gaps, and so the spread, do not.

stem: Five readings, 43, 47, 50, 54 and 56, were all 3 too high. Compare the mean and spread before and after correcting them.

steps.decision: From the five readings as recorded.
Each value 3 lower: the mean falls by 3, the spread is unchanged.

prompt: Every reading in a set was 3 too high. The recorded standard deviation was 5.1. What is the standard deviation of the corrected readings?
options: It cannot be found without the readings
explain: As in step 2 of See it, moving every value by the same amount moves the mean but none of the gaps, so the standard deviation stays 5.1.

twin.prompt: Every mass in a set was 0.5 kg too light. The recorded standard deviation was 1.4 kg. What is the corrected standard deviation?
options: It cannot be found without the masses
twin.explain: Adding 0.5 kg to every mass moves the mean only; the spread stays 1.4 kg.

optionNotes.why: That adds the 0.5 kg to the spread. The gaps between masses are unchanged.

optionNotes.option: It cannot be found without the masses
optionNotes.why: A shift of every value leaves the spread as it was, so the masses are not needed.
That takes the 3 off the standard deviation too. The gaps between readings have not changed, so neither has the spread.

optionNotes.option: It cannot be found without the readings
optionNotes.why: It can: shifting every reading by 3 leaves every gap, and so the spread, exactly as it was.

text: Which way should the answer move?

md: Before you calculate, predict. A value below the mean that leaves pulls the mean up; one above it pulls the mean down. A value far from the mean that leaves makes the spread smaller, and one far away that joins makes it bigger. An answer that moves the other way has a slip in it.

stem: Check the directions of the runners and the seedlings above against their answers.

steps.working: 61 left a set with mean 50: the mean falls, to 49
steps.decision: The value was above the mean.

steps.working: 61 was 11 from the mean, far more than a typical 6: the spread falls, to 5.22
steps.decision: A far value leaving narrows the set.

steps.working: 23 joined a set with mean 14 and spread 2: both rise, to 15 and 3.40
steps.decision: A far value joining widens it.

prompt: A value of 33 is added to a set with a mean of 42 and a standard deviation of 5. Which way does the mean move?
options: Up, because there are more values
It stays the same, because one value cannot move it
explain: As in step 3 of See it, compare the value with the mean: a value below the mean pulls it down when it joins.

twin.prompt: A value of 70 is removed from a set with a mean of 55. Which way does the mean move?
options: Up, because there are fewer values
It stays the same, because one value cannot move it
twin.explain: Taking out a value above the mean pulls the mean down.

optionNotes.option: Up, because there are fewer values
optionNotes.why: The count falls, but what decides the direction is that 70 was above the mean.

optionNotes.option: It stays the same, because one value cannot move it
optionNotes.why: Only removing a value equal to the mean leaves it unchanged.

optionNotes.option: Up, because there are more values
optionNotes.why: The count rises, but the mean moves towards the new value, and 33 is below 42.

optionNotes.option: It stays the same, because one value cannot move it
optionNotes.why: Only a value equal to the mean leaves it unchanged; 33 is 9 below it.

text: Going further: two changes at once

md: Sometimes one value is corrected and another struck out. Make the changes one at a time on the totals, move the count only for the value that leaves, and recompute once at the end. Totals add and subtract in any order, so either change can come first.

title: Where this specification stops
md: A sample standard deviation, dividing by $n - 1$, is not on this specification, and a grouped table cannot be corrected value by value: its individual values were never recorded.

stem: 10 values had a mean of 24 and a standard deviation of 5. The value 18 should have been 27, and the value 35 is struck out. Find the new mean and standard deviation.

steps.decision: Rebuild both totals.
Swap the corrected value, then take out the one struck out.
The same moves with the squares. Only the strike-out moves the count: $n = 9$.
Recompute once, keeping more of the mean than you print.

prompt: 12 values have $\sum x = 300$. The value 20 should have been 26, and the value 31 is struck out. What is the new mean?
explain: As in steps 2 and 4 of See it: $\dfrac{300 - 20 + 26 - 31}{11} = \dfrac{275}{11} = 25$. Only the strike-out moves the count, from 12 to 11.

twin.prompt: 16 values have $\sum x = 512$. The value 22 should have been 31, and the value 41 is struck out. What is the new mean?

md:
Name the change first: only a removal or an addition moves the count.
Rebuild $\sum x = n\bar{x}$ and $\sum x^{2} = n\left(\sigma^{2} + \bar{x}^{2}\right)$.
Edit $\sum x$ by the values and $\sum x^{2}$ by their squares, both values in a correction.
Recompute the mean with the right count, and use that mean in the formula.
Predict the direction; a shift of every value moves the mean, never the spread.

Summer 2025 Q5 corrected one value: three marks for the corrected mean, four for the corrected standard deviation, the second part one of the hardest on that paper.
